heinous

HAY-nus -- rhymes loosely with 'famous.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Heinous is utterly evil or wicked.

The judge called the crime heinous, one of the most brutal cases the court had ever seen.

Example

Investigators describe a crime so heinous, so brutal and shocking, that even experienced detectives are disturbed reading the case file.

That shocking, extreme wickedness is exactly what heinous describes. Unlike 'unfortunate,' which can describe any bad luck, heinous specifically emphasizes moral horror.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

atrocious: Atrocious can condemn wickedness, but in everyday use it just as often means shockingly bad in quality -- atrocious handwriting, an atrocious performance. Heinous never softens that way: a heinous act is utterly evil, never merely sloppy or poorly done.

abominable: Abominable describes something that causes moral disgust, something people recoil from as hateful or loathsome. Heinous points more narrowly at wicked acts themselves: a heinous crime shocks the conscience, while abominable can also condemn conditions, treatment, or behavior that repels us.

vile: Vile stresses how disgusting and low something is, turning the stomach as much as the conscience. Heinous stresses moral horror instead: a heinous deed is judged utterly evil, while a vile one is judged repulsive and degrading.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

admirable: deserving respect and approval

virtuous: having high moral standards

Where it sits · how morally shocking the act is — cruel → heinous → monstrous

cruel vs. heinous: Cruel is a far milder charge than heinous: a cruel act deliberately causes suffering, but heinous is saved for acts so utterly evil that they shock everyone who hears of them.

monstrous vs. heinous: Monstrous can feel even stronger than heinous: heinous focuses on the shocking wickedness of an act, while monstrous suggests something so evil it seems almost inhuman.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hein-/hain-

root — hein-/hain-: hatred (Old French (haine, hair 'to hate'))

Put it together

Put it together: Heinous comes from Old French haineus, 'hateful,' rooted in haine, 'hatred,' itself connected to the same ancient Germanic root behind the English word hate. Something heinous, at its root, inspires hatred -- it is so wicked that it provokes moral outrage.

Use the root in a new word: hate

Use the root in a new word: hate: It's easy to hate a villain who shows no remorse for the harm he has caused.
